contribution: Linear model and direct proportionality in motion: the slope of the $(t, s)$ graph is the speed, the distance (not the position) is directly proportional to time, and the equation $s = s_0 + vt$ works as a calculation tool, for example for the distance of the Voyager 2 probe (a model value, source NASA/JPL).
learn: calculate the distance, time or speed in uniform motion with the formula $s = s_0 + vt$.
read the speed and the initial position from a $(t, s)$ graph.
explain when the distance is directly proportional to time and when the position is.
prior: A straight line is fitted to measurement points, and its slope tells you how much $y$ changes when $x$ increases by one (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*)
In the equation of a straight line, the constant term is where the line crosses the $y$-axis (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*)

activities.text: The Voyager 2 probe left the Earth in 1977. In November 2018 it crossed the heliopause, the boundary beyond which the Sun's solar wind no longer dominates space. According to NASA's JPL, the probe was then 119.7 AU from the Sun, and it is still moving away at a speed of $15.341\,\text{km/s}$. The astronomical unit AU is roughly the distance between the Earth and the Sun. You cannot hold a ruler next to the probe, but you can still give its distance for any day.
activities.question: What information do you need to calculate the distance of the probe from the Sun, say a year from now, and what do you assume about its speed?

activities.title: Recap: the slope of a line
activities.prompt: The measurement points (time, position) lie on a straight line in the $(t, s)$ coordinate system. What does the slope of the line tell you?

choices.text: The point where the line crosses the $s$-axis.
choices.feedback: That is the starting point of the line, not the slope (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*). The slope tells you how steep the line is: by how many units $s$ changes when $t$ increases by one.

choices.text: How much the position changes per unit of time.
choices.feedback: Correct. The slope is $\Delta s : \Delta t$ (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*). In motion it is the speed, and you apply it today.

choices.text: How long the line is.
choices.feedback: The length of the line does not matter, because the line continues in both directions. The slope is the ratio of two changes, $\Delta s : \Delta t$ (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*).

activities.title: Prediction 1: the shape of the graph
activities.prompt: A trolley starts from the zero point and moves uniformly at $2.0\,\text{m/s}$. What does its $(t, s)$ graph look like, when the time $t$ is on the horizontal axis and the position $s$ on the vertical axis?

choices.text: A horizontal line, because the speed does not change.
choices.feedback: The values of the model rule this out: the position increases by $2.0\,\text{m}$ every second, for example at $4.0\,\text{s}$ it is $8.0\,\text{m}$. A horizontal line would describe an object that stays in place.

choices.text: A rising straight line through the origin.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: the position is $2.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot t$, for example $4.0\,\text{m}$ at $2.0\,\text{s}$ and $8.0\,\text{m}$ at $4.0\,\text{s}$. The time doubles and the position doubles, so the points lie on a line that starts from the origin.

choices.text: A curve bending upwards, because the distance keeps growing.
choices.feedback: The values of the model rule this out: the position increases by the same amount, $2.0\,\text{m}$, every second, so the graph does not curve. The distance keeps growing, but steadily. A curve would mean that the speed changes.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the time doubles
activities.prompt: A trolley starts at $s_0 = 6.0\,\text{m}$ and moves at $2.0\,\text{m/s}$. At $t = 2.0\,\text{s}$ its position is $10\,\text{m}$. Where is the trolley at $t = 4.0\,\text{s}$, when the time is doubled?

choices.text: $20\,\text{m}$, because the time doubles and the position doubles.
choices.feedback: The values of the model rule this out: at $4.0\,\text{s}$ the position is $14\,\text{m}$. Only the distance $\Delta s = vt$ is directly proportional to time, and it grows from $4.0\,\text{m}$ to $8.0\,\text{m}$. The position does not double, because the motion started from $6.0\,\text{m}$.

The values of the model support this: $s = 6.0\,\text{m} + 2.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot 4.0\,\text{s} = 14\,\text{m}$. The distance doubled ($4.0\,\text{m}$ became $8.0\,\text{m}$), but the position did not, because the initial position $6.0\,\text{m}$ stays in the sum.

choices.text: $12\,\text{m}$, because the speed is $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ and so the position grows by $2.0\,\text{m}$.
choices.feedback: The values of the model rule this out. The speed $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ is the distance in one second. The interval $2.0\,\text{s}$…$4.0\,\text{s}$ is two seconds long, so the trolley travels $4.0\,\text{m}$ and the position is $10\,\text{m} + 4.0\,\text{m} = 14\,\text{m}$.

activities.text: A trolley moves along a straight track at constant speed. Change the initial position and the speed, start the motion or drag the moment, and see how the $(t, s)$ graph is drawn.
activities.howto: Set the initial position $s_0$ and the speed $v$ with the sliders; the time returns to zero. *Start* plays the motion, *Pause* stops it and *Reset* returns to the beginning. You can also drag the *Moment* slider. On the track, the orange vertical lines are the positions of the trolley at whole seconds, the green flag is the initial position and the arrow shows the speed. A straight line is drawn in the graph up to the moment you have reached. When you have reached the moment $6\,\text{s}$, a slope triangle appears in the graph. *Speed (replay)* changes only the pace of the replay.
activities.model: The trolley moves along a straight track at constant speed: no friction and no acceleration, and the full speed is reached right at the start. The positions on the track and the values in the graph are values calculated by the model, not measurements. The trolley moves in one direction only, so the speed is positive.
activities.calc: The position is $s = s_0 + vt$ and the distance travelled is $\Delta s = s - s_0 = vt$. The slope triangle in the graph goes from the moment $t = 2\,\text{s}$ to the moment $t = 6\,\text{s}$, so $\Delta t = 4.0\,\text{s}$, and the slope $\Delta s : \Delta t$ is the speed $v$.

activities.title: Experiment 1: starting from the zero point
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The initial position $s_0 = 0$ and the speed $v = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$ stay constant. Change only the moment $t$ and record the position at at least three moments $t > 0$, for example $2.0\,\text{s}$, $4.0\,\text{s}$ and $8.0\,\text{s}$. For each row, calculate the quotient $s : t$. Also look at how the graph is drawn.

question.prompt: What happens to the quotients $s : t$ as the moment $t$ increases?

choices.text: They are all the same, and they equal the speed.
choices.feedback: Correct. When the motion starts from the zero point, $s : t = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$ in every row, for example $4.0\,\text{m} : 2.0\,\text{s}$ and $8.0\,\text{m} : 4.0\,\text{s}$. The position is then directly proportional to time, and the ratio is the speed.

choices.text: They increase, because the position increases.
choices.feedback: The position increases, but the time increases too: double the time gives double the position, so the ratio does not change. Calculate for example $4.0 : 2.0$ and $8.0 : 4.0$.

choices.text: They decrease, because the time grows in the divisor.
choices.feedback: The time grows, but at the same time the position grows in the same proportion. Calculate the quotients from the rows of the table: they are all equal.

activities.title: Experiment 2: starting from 6.0 metres
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. Now the initial position is $s_0 = 6.0\,\text{m}$ and the speed is still $2.0\,\text{m/s}$. Change only the moment $t$ and record the position $s$ and the distance $\Delta s$ at at least three moments $t > 0$, for example $2.0\,\text{s}$, $4.0\,\text{s}$ and $8.0\,\text{s}$. For both columns, calculate the quotient (position or distance) divided by the time $t$.

question.prompt: Which quantity is directly proportional to time when $s_0 = 6.0\,\text{m}$?

choices.text: The distance $\Delta s$: the quotient $\Delta s : t$ is the same in every row, $2.0\,\text{m/s}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. For example $4.0\,\text{m} : 2.0\,\text{s} = 8.0\,\text{m} : 4.0\,\text{s} = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$. The quotient of the position $s : t$ changes ($10 : 2.0 = 5.0$, but $14 : 4.0 = 3.5$), so the position is not directly proportional to time.

choices.text: The position $s$, because it is on the vertical axis of the graph.
choices.feedback: A quantity on the vertical axis is not automatically proportional to time. Calculate the quotients $s : t$: they are different ($10 : 2.0 = 5.0$ and $14 : 4.0 = 3.5$), so the ratio is not constant.

choices.text: Both, because the motion is uniform.
choices.feedback: Being uniform is not enough: the position is proportional to time only when the initial position is zero. Here $s : t$ varies ($5.0$ and $3.5$), although $\Delta s : t$ is constant.

activities.title: Conclusion: when is the distance proportional to time?
activities.prompt: Write, based on your tables: when is the position directly proportional to time, and when only the distance? What does the quotient $\Delta s : t$ tell you about the motion?
activities.model: In experiment 1 the initial position was zero, and the quotient of position and time $s : t$ was $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ in every row, which is the speed: the position was directly proportional to time. In experiment 2 the initial position was $6.0\,\text{m}$. The quotient of the position changed, for example $10 : 2.0 = 5.0\,\text{m/s}$ and $14 : 4.0 = 3.5\,\text{m/s}$, but the quotient of the distance $\Delta s : t$ was $2.0\,\text{m/s}$ in every row. So the distance travelled is always directly proportional to time, and the position only when the initial position is zero. The quotient $\Delta s : t$ is the speed. The values are values calculated by the model: the model assumes constant speed and no friction.
criteria: I said that the position is proportional to time only when the initial position is zero.
I used the numbers in the table to compare the quotients $s : t$ and $\Delta s : t$.
I said that the quotient $\Delta s : t$ is the speed.
I mentioned that the values are model values.

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the experiments. Then return to the question at the start: what information is needed to calculate the distance of Voyager 2 for a future day, and what is assumed about its speed?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student solves a problem: a trolley starts at $s_0 = 5.0\,\text{m}$ and moves at $3.0\,\text{m/s}$. Where is it at $t = 6.0\,\text{s}$? The student calculates: “At $2.0\,\text{s}$ the position is $5.0\,\text{m} + 3.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot 2.0\,\text{s} = 11\,\text{m}$. The time $6.0\,\text{s}$ is three times as much, so the position is $3 \cdot 11\,\text{m} = 33\,\text{m}$.” Where is the error?

choices.text: The position is not directly proportional to time, because the initial position is not zero. The correct result is $s = 5.0\,\text{m} + 3.0\,\text{m/s} \cdot 6.0\,\text{s} = 23\,\text{m}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. Only the distance $\Delta s = vt$ triples ($6.0\,\text{m}$ becomes $18\,\text{m}$), and the initial position is added once: $5.0 + 18 = 23\,\text{m}$. The error could have been noticed by reasoning: the trolley cannot be more than $30\,\text{m}$ away, because in $6.0\,\text{s}$ it travels only $18\,\text{m}$.

choices.text: The speed should be converted to kilometres per hour before substituting.
choices.feedback: No conversion is needed: the speed is already in m/s and the time in seconds, so the units are compatible. The error is in the reasoning, where the position is multiplied by three.

choices.text: Triple the time also triples the speed, so the position should be even greater.
choices.feedback: The speed does not change, because the motion is uniform: it is $3.0\,\text{m/s}$ all the time. The time triples, and so the distance triples, but the initial position does not.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation, because in uniform motion the position and the time are proportional.
choices.feedback: When the initial position is not zero, the distance is proportional to time, but the position is not. Check by substituting $t = 6.0\,\text{s}$ directly: $5.0 + 3.0 \cdot 6.0 = 23\,\text{m}$, not $33\,\text{m}$.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: At time $0\,\text{s}$ a cyclist is already $120\,\text{m}$ from the starting line and rides away from it uniformly at $21.6\,\text{km/h}$. How far from the starting line is the cyclist $45\,\text{s}$ later? Give the answer in metres.
hints: What is the initial position, and what is the speed? Are the units compatible?
Use the formula $s = s_0 + vt$. First convert the speed to m/s by substituting $1\,\text{km} = 1000\,\text{m}$ and $1\,\text{h} = 3600\,\text{s}$.

mistakes.feedback: You used the speed 21.6 directly as metres per second. First convert by substitution: $21.6\,\text{km/h} = \dfrac{21.6\cdot1000\,\text{m}}{3600\,\text{s}} = 6.0\,\text{m/s}$.
You calculated only the distance travelled $vt$. At the start of the interval the cyclist was already $120\,\text{m}$ from the starting line, so the position is $s_0 + vt$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** initial position $s_0 = 120\,\text{m}$, speed $v = 21.6\,\text{km/h}$, time $t = 45\,\text{s}$

**Find:** position $s$ from the starting line in metres

**Principle:** The speed of the cyclist is constant, so the motion is uniform, and the position follows the linear model. The initial position is not zero, so it must be added to the distance travelled.

**Formula:** $s = s_0 + vt$

**Conversions:** Substitute $1\,\text{km} = 1000\,\text{m}$ and $1\,\text{h} = 3600\,\text{s}$: $v = 21.6\,\text{km/h} = \dfrac{21.6\cdot1000\,\text{m}}{3600\,\text{s}} = 6.0\,\text{m/s}$. The time and the initial position are already in SI units.

**Substitution:** $s = 120\,\text{m} + 6.0\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \cdot 45\,\text{s} = 120\,\text{m} + 270\,\text{m} = 390\,\text{m}$

**Answer:** $390\,\text{m}$, two significant figures as in the time $45\,\text{s}$.

**Reasonableness:** The speed $6\,\text{m/s}$ is about $22\,\text{km/h}$, and $45\,\text{s}$ is three quarters of a minute, so the distance travelled is about $6 \cdot 45 \approx 270\,\text{m}$. The initial position $120\,\text{m}$ is added to this, and the position is greater than the initial position, as it should be when the cyclist moves away.

activities.text: Practise at three levels. The Level 1 exercises use the formula directly, the Level 2 exercises involve converting units or using an initial position, and Level 3 requires reasoning, for example calculating the distance of the Voyager 2 probe.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: An object moves uniformly, and its $(t, s)$ graph is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The position $s$ is directly proportional to the time $t$.
choices.feedback: The graph of a directly proportional quantity passes through the origin, because the ratio $s : t$ is constant. Here the line starts from $s_0 \neq 0$, so the ratio $s : t$ changes with time.

choices.text: The distance travelled $\Delta s = s - s_0$ is directly proportional to the time $t$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The line is equally steep everywhere, so $\Delta s = vt$ and the ratio $\Delta s : t = v$ is constant. When the initial position $s_0$ is subtracted from the position $s$, the remaining distance is proportional to time.

choices.text: The object does not move uniformly, because the line does not pass through the origin.
choices.feedback: The mark of uniform motion is a straight line, not that the line passes through the origin. A line that does not pass through the origin describes uniform motion that starts from $s_0$: $s = s_0 + vt$.

activities.title: 2. Interpreting a graph
activities.prompt: The $(t, s)$ graph of an object is a horizontal line at $s = 4\,\text{m}$. What is the object doing?

choices.text: The object moves at a constant speed of $4\,\text{m/s}$.
choices.feedback: This is tempting, because a horizontal line in a $(t, v)$ graph means constant speed. Here, however, the vertical axis shows the position $s$, not the speed. The speed is the slope of the $(t, s)$ graph, and the slope of a horizontal line is zero.

choices.text: The object is at rest at $s = 4\,\text{m}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The position does not change as time passes, so $\Delta s = 0$ and the speed is $v = \Delta s : \Delta t = 0$. The slope of a horizontal line is zero.

choices.text: The object moves uniformly, because the graph is a straight line.
choices.feedback: The $(t, s)$ graph of uniform motion is a straight line, but a straight line alone does not tell whether the object moves. The speed is the slope of the line, $\Delta s : \Delta t$, and in a horizontal line $\Delta s = 0$, so the speed is zero.

activities.title: 3. Reading a graph
activities.prompt: The line of a $(t, s)$ graph of uniform motion passes through the points $(1.0\,\text{s};\ 7.0\,\text{m})$ and $(5.0\,\text{s};\ 19\,\text{m})$. What is the initial position $s_0$ of the motion? Give the answer in metres.
hints: The initial position is the position at time $t = 0$, that is, the point where the line crosses the $s$-axis. What is the slope of the line?
The slope is $v = \dfrac{s_2 - s_1}{t_2 - t_1}$. You get the initial position by going back in time from the point $(t_1, s_1)$ to the start: $s_0 = s_1 - v t_1$.

mistakes.feedback: You read the position at time $t = 1.0\,\text{s}$. The initial position is the position at time $t = 0$, so you must extend the line back by one second, $3.0\,\text{m}$ downwards.
You calculated the slope of the line, that is, the speed $3.0\,\text{m/s}$. The initial position is where the line crosses the $s$-axis, $s_0 = s_1 - v t_1$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** points $(t_1, s_1) = (1.0\,\text{s};\ 7.0\,\text{m})$ and $(t_2, s_2) = (5.0\,\text{s};\ 19\,\text{m})$ on the same line

**Find:** initial position $s_0$, that is, the position at time $t = 0$, in metres

**Principle:** The motion is uniform, so the line of the $(t, s)$ graph follows the equation $s = s_0 + vt$. The slope of the line is the speed, and the point where the line crosses the $s$-axis is the initial position.

**Reading the graph:** The two given points are enough. The change in position between them is divided by the time interval, which gives the slope. Then we go back from the first point to the moment $t = 0$: in one second the position decreases by $v \cdot 1.0\,\text{s}$.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{s_2 - s_1}{t_2 - t_1}$ and $s_1 = s_0 + v t_1$, so $s_0 = s_1 - v t_1$

**Conversions:** None needed: the positions are in metres and the times in seconds.

**Substitution:** $v = \dfrac{19\,\text{m} - 7.0\,\text{m}}{5.0\,\text{s} - 1.0\,\text{s}} = 3.0\,\text{m/s}$ and $s_0 = 7.0\,\text{m} - 3.0\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \cdot 1.0\,\text{s} = 4.0\,\text{m}$

**Answer:** $4.0\,\text{m}$, two significant figures as in the positions $7.0\,\text{m}$ and $19\,\text{m}$.

**Reasonableness:** Check with the second point: $s = 4.0\,\text{m} + 3.0\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \cdot 5.0\,\text{s} = 19\,\text{m}$, which is the given value. The initial position is smaller than $7.0\,\text{m}$, as it should be, because the object moves forwards.

activities.title: 4. Explain and evaluate the model
activities.prompt: Explain why the distance of the Voyager 2 probe from the Sun can be calculated with a linear model, and why the calculated value is a model value and not a measurement.
criteria: I wrote the equation $s = s_0 + vt$ and named its quantities.
I said that the model assumes the speed is constant.
I justified why the value is a model value: the speed is not exactly constant, because the Sun's gravity slows the probe.
I compared the model with the JPL value.
activities.model: The speed of the probe is almost constant, so its distance from the Sun grows by the same amount every second: $s = s_0 + vt$, where $s_0 = 119.7\,\text{AU}$ at the moment of the heliopause crossing on 5 November 2018 and $v = 15.341\,\text{km/s}$. With this model the distance on 5 November 2026 is about $145.6\,\text{AU}$. The value is a model value, because the speed is not exactly constant: the Sun's gravity slows the probe slightly. For 15 February 2026 the model gives $143.3\,\text{AU}$, while JPL reports $143.05\,\text{AU}$ for February 2026. The difference is about $0.2\,\text{AU}$. The difference is partly because the Sun's gravity slows the probe slightly and the initial distance is given only to the nearest tenth. The model is accurate to a fraction of a percent, so it is good for studying a few years.

activities.text: Finally, one quick question. Answer first on your own and only then open the answer.
